title: Air India to Restore Most Suspended International Flights From September 2026
excerpt: Tata Group-backed carrier says June-August capacity cuts were always temporary, with most routes already on sale for September — but Chicago and Washington will remain grounded due to aircraft shortages.
body:
• Air India expects to restore most temporarily suspended domestic and international flights from September 2026, with the majority of the September schedule already on sale.
  • Services to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles will remain suspended due to aircraft shortages from the fleet retrofit programme and delayed new deliveries.
  • Europe-bound operations are expected to normalise from September, and Newark will regain additional frequencies as capacity returns.
  • Pakistan's continuing airspace closure remains the airline's biggest operational challenge, though the reopening of Iranian and Iraqi airspace would provide significant relief.
  • New Airbus A350-1000 deliveries are expected towards the end of 2026.

Air India has confirmed that the majority of its temporarily suspended international and domestic flights will be restored from September, marking the end of a difficult summer of capacity cuts that left travellers scrambling for alternatives on long-haul routes to North America, Europe, and Asia.

Nipun Aggarwal, Air India's Chief Commercial and Transformation Officer and Chairman of Air India Express, made the announcement on the sidelines of a tourism conference organised by the Federation of Associations in Indian Tourism & Hospitality (FAITH) on Friday.

September Schedule Already on Sale

"We have cut the capacity only for June, July and August. From September onwards, most of the flights are already on sale," Aggarwal said, stressing that the rationalisation was always planned as a short-term measure and that September services were never withdrawn from the reservation system.

The restoration is welcome news for the millions of diaspora travellers who rely on Air India for direct connections between India and destinations across five continents. The airline continued to operate more than 1,200 international flights monthly even during the cuts, but reduced frequencies on high-demand routes to San Francisco, Toronto, Paris, Melbourne, Sydney, and Singapore, while suspending services to Chicago and Shanghai outright.

""The order is already placed," Aggarwal said."

Chicago and Washington Still Grounded

Not all routes will return in September. Services to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles will remain suspended due to a shortage of wide-body aircraft. Aggarwal attributed the gap to three converging pressures: several wide-body aircraft undergoing cabin retrofit as part of Air India's ongoing transformation programme, the retirement of older Boeing 777-200LR aircraft, and delays in new aircraft deliveries.

"The aircraft that we were supposed to get have been delayed. The old aircraft were retired," he said, adding that deliveries of new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft are expected to commence towards the end of the year.

Newark Liberty International Airport will regain additional frequencies as capacity returns, and European operations are expected to normalise progressively through August ahead of a full September resumption.

Airspace Challenges Persist

The continuing closure of Pakistan's airspace remains the single biggest operational challenge for Air India, according to Aggarwal. Flights to Europe and North America have been forced onto longer routings to avoid restricted zones, burning more fuel and adding hours to journey times.

"The airline continues to rebalance its network wherever possible, but there is little it can do beyond adapting schedules until the geopolitical situation improves," Aggarwal said, noting that the reopening of Iranian and Iraqi airspace would provide "significant relief."

The airspace constraints, combined with record international jet fuel prices, were the primary reasons Air India announced the capacity rationalisation in May. Rather than risk last-minute cancellations during the busy summer season, the airline chose to trim frequencies and suspend a handful of routes — a move that reduced long-haul flying by roughly 10 to 12 per cent at peak.

Impact on Travellers and Fares

Domestic capacity reductions, which peaked at 10 to 15 per cent, are already being wound back. Aggarwal said demand remains strong, particularly in the domestic market, and has not been materially affected despite the temporary network changes.

On the question that matters most to flyers — ticket prices — Aggarwal offered cautious optimism. "As supply comes back, as oil prices cool down, airfares will cool down as well," he said, adding that Air India has not altered its pricing structure and that fares are ultimately determined by market demand and supply.

For NRI travellers, particularly those in the United States who have seen fewer direct options and higher fares this summer, the restoration cannot come soon enough. Industry observers note that even with Air India's return to fuller schedules, airspace restrictions will continue to inflate operating costs on key corridors until geopolitical tensions in the Middle East ease.

What's Next

Air India's aircraft acquisition plans remain on track despite the airspace turbulence. "The order is already placed," Aggarwal said. The airline has one of the largest outstanding aircraft orders in global aviation, including A350-1000 wide-bodies that will eventually allow it to restore and expand its long-haul network. The immediate priority will be bringing September schedules fully online and demonstrating to passengers that the summer disruptions were a one-off, not a new normal.
image_caption: An Air India Boeing 777 photographed during flight approach against a clear sky. The airline is restoring most of its suspended international capacity from September after a summer of cuts driven by airspace closures and high fuel costs.
nri_angle: Indian diaspora travelers, particularly NRIs in the US and Europe, have faced flight cancellations, elevated fares, and routing disruptions all summer. The September restoration means most long-haul routes to Europe and key US cities will return, though those relying on Chicago and Washington connections will need to plan alternatives.
author: Diaspora Desk
